c.tagline: Japan's cosmopolitan port city of marbled beef, mountain views, and old foreign quarters.

taxi.fareNote: Metered; ride-hailing is limited in Japan - apps like GO, DiDi and Uber dispatch licensed taxis rather than private drivers, and there is no informal street bargaining.

emergency.note: 110 reaches the police; 119 is for fire and ambulance.

avoid.reason: Minor bar-tout hustle in the Sannomiya nightlife district late at night.

hood_desc: Kobe's downtown transport hub and main shopping-and-eating district, where JR, Hankyu, Hanshin, subway, and Port Liner lines all meet; covered arcades, department stores, and izakaya make it the obvious base.

The hillside quarter of Kitano-cho, lined with the Ijinkan - the Western-style mansions of 19th-century foreign traders, such as the Weathercock House - now home to cafes, boutiques, and viewpoints over the city.
A long shopping arcade rolling down to Nankinmachi, Kobe's compact, lantern-strung Chinatown packed with street-food stalls and dim sum; the city's liveliest place to browse and graze.
Kobe's redeveloped waterfront of the red Port Tower, the Maritime Museum, a Ferris wheel, and the umie mall; a breezy, illuminated place for a harbourside evening out.

An eastern district famous as one of Japan's great sake-brewing regions, with historic breweries and tasting halls along the coast, plus the ferries and stadium at nearby Rokko Island; quieter and residential.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink everywhere.

transit.hours: Subways and trains run roughly 5:30am to just past midnight, with no regular overnight service; night buses and taxis fill the gap after the last trains.
transit.note: Kobe is stitched together by JR and the private Hankyu and Hanshin lines, the Kobe Municipal Subway (Seishin-Yamate and Kaigan lines), and the automated Port Liner linking Sannomiya to Port Island and the airport; the retro City Loop and Port Loop buses connect the main sights.
transit.pay: Buy an ICOCA or PiTaPa IC card from station machines and tap in and out, or tap a contactless card at some gates; subway base fares start around ¥210 (~$1.40) and rise with distance. Day passes cover the tourist loop buses.

transit.m: Kobe-Kanku Bay Shuttle ferry from Kansai Airport (~30 min)

food.name: Kobe beef steak
food.desc: Certified Tajima-strain wagyu, cooked on a teppan in front of you and served in small portions with garlic chips and mustard.

places.name: Steakland Kobe
places.note: Teppanyaki counter with the most affordable certified Kobe beef sets in town.

places.name: Mouriya
places.note: Long-established Kobe beef house running since the 1880s, several grades offered.

places.name: Ishida
places.note: Popular teppanyaki restaurant in the old foreign quarter; book ahead.

food.name: Sobameshi
food.desc: Nagata working-class dish: yakisoba noodles chopped and stir-fried into rice with sauce, often topped with stewed beef tendon.

places.name: Okonomiyaki Aomori
places.note: Widely named as the originating shop for sobameshi.

places.name: Nagata Tank-suji
places.note: The best-known place to try it centrally, busy with locals and visitors.

places.name: Hakusan Okonomiyaki
places.note: Many sobameshi and okonomiyaki variants; open 11am-9pm, closed Tuesdays.

food.name: Bokkake okonomiyaki
food.desc: Kobe okonomiyaki topped with bokkake - beef tendon and konjac stewed for hours until sticky and sweet-savoury.

places.name: Nagata Tank-suji
places.note: Bokkake is the house signature alongside the sobameshi.

places.name: Hakusan Okonomiyaki
places.note: Griddle counter covering the full Kobe okonomiyaki repertoire.

places.name: Okonomiyaki Aomori
places.note: Neighbourhood original where the tendon topping belongs.

food.name: Akashiyaki
food.desc: Featherlight egg-rich octopus dumplings from nearby Akashi, served by the dozen and dipped in warm dashi rather than sauce.

places.name: Tako-an
places.note: Recommended spot in Kobe for akashiyaki; fragrant dashi, melting texture.

places.name: Uontana shopping street
places.note: Short train ride west; the fish-market street where the dish was born.

places.name: Motomachi arcade stalls
places.note: Covered shopping arcade with counters selling akashiyaki and takoyaki.

food.name: Butaman pork buns
food.desc: Steamed pork buns from Kobe's Chinatown, small enough to eat two or three standing up in the square.

places.name: Roushouki
places.note: Founded 1915; the queue outside is the landmark, buns sold in threes.

places.name: Yunyun
places.note: Second-generation shop on the same square, known for buns and dumplings.

places.name: Nankinmachi square stalls
places.note: Ring of street counters selling buns, croquettes and Kobe beef skewers.

food.name: Kobe Western pastries
food.desc: Legacy of the port's foreign residents: baumkuchen, butter biscuits and cheesecake from bakeries founded by German settlers.

places.name: Freundlieb
places.note: German bakery inside a converted church; famous butter biscuits and sandwiches.

places.name: Juchheim
places.note: Baumkuchen house started by a German baker who settled in Kobe.

places.name: Kitano-zaka pastry shops
places.note: Hillside street of patisseries in the old foreign-residence quarter.

food.name: Nada sake
food.desc: Kobe's Nada Gogo is Japan's largest sake region, using Rokko mountain water and Yamada Nishiki rice for crisp, dry styles.

places.name: Hakutsuru Sake Brewery Museum
places.note: Taisho-era brewhouse preserved with English displays and tasting at the shop.

places.name: Kikumasamune Sake Museum
places.note: Wooden-plaster brewery museum; barrel workshop across the road by reservation.

places.name: Sakuramasamune Kinenkan
places.note: Brewery museum and restaurant on the Nada sake road walking route.

food.name: Kissaten coffee
food.desc: Kobe was one of Japan's first coffee ports and still runs old-school kissaten pouring careful hand-drip in china cups.

places.name: Nishimura Coffee
places.note: Kobe institution since 1948; the Nakayamate main store is the one to visit.

places.name: Cafe Freundlieb
places.note: Coffee and cake in the upstairs hall of the converted church bakery.

landmarks: Kobe Port Tower
This crimson hyperboloid lattice tower, elegantly renovated with a rooftop deck, has symbolised Kobe's harbour skyline since 1963.
Kitano Ijinkan District
Hillside streets of preserved Meiji-era Western mansions, built by foreign merchants after the port opened in 1868, exude Kobe's cosmopolitan heritage.
Mount Rokko
Cable cars climb to gardens, a music box museum and the Ten Million Dollar Night View, Japan's most celebrated urban panorama.
Nunobiki Herb Gardens and Ropeway
A scenic gondola soars over waterfalls to terraced herb gardens, glasshouses and sweeping city-and-bay views on Kobe's forested slopes.
Meriken Park
Waterfront lawns showcase the Port Tower, the sail-shaped Maritime Museum and the photogenic BE KOBE monument beside the cruise piers.
Nankinmachi (Kobe Chinatown)
Lantern-strung gates open onto a compact grid of steaming street-food stalls, one of Japan's three great Chinatowns since the 1860s.
Arima Onsen
Tucked behind Mount Rokko, one of Japan's oldest hot-spring towns pairs iron-rich gold waters with lantern-lit lanes and ryokan tradition.
Ikuta Shrine
Founded in the 3rd century and predating the city itself, this vermilion shrine hides a serene sacred forest steps from bustling Sannomiya.
Hakutsuru Sake Brewery Museum
In the famed Nada sake district, this preserved wooden brewery demonstrates traditional brewing and pours free tastings of Kobe's signature drink.
Port of Kobe Earthquake Memorial Park
A preserved section of quake-buckled quay commemorates the devastating 1995 Great Hanshin Earthquake and the city's remarkable recovery.

train.note: Japan is an island network with no international trains. The San'yo Shinkansen runs west from Shin-Kobe toward Okayama, Hiroshima and Hakata, and east via the Tokaido Shinkansen to Kyoto, Nagoya and Tokyo - book bullet trains on JR West or JR Central's smartEX. Note that Shin-Kobe is a separate station from the main city hub at Sannomiya, linked by a short subway ride. Local JR, Hankyu and Hanshin lines reach Osaka in about 20-30 minutes for a few hundred yen.

bus.note: There are no international buses from Japan. Willer Express (https://willerexpress.com/en/) and the JR Bus group run extensive highway and overnight coach networks from the Sannomiya bus terminal to Tokyo, Kyoto, Hiroshima and Kyushu. Sannomiya is right in the centre, so coaches are convenient here; overnight runs to Tokyo take about 9 hours and are far cheaper than the Shinkansen.

ferry.note: Kobe has no scheduled international passenger ferries, but its port is a major domestic hub. MOL Sunflower runs an overnight ship from the Sannomiya terminal to Oita in Kyushu, arriving next morning, while the Jumbo Ferry crosses to Takamatsu and Shodoshima several times a day and overnight. The Kobe-Kanku Bay Shuttle reaches Kansai International Airport in about 30 minutes, a fast alternative to the airport bus. Cabins and cars on the Kyushu boat should be booked ahead in holiday periods.

half.name: Mt Rokko
half.blurb: The green mountain wall above the city, with a cable car, gardens, and the famous 'ten-million-dollar' night view over Kobe.

half.name: Nada Sake District
half.blurb: Historic sake breweries with tasting museums along the eastern shore, in Japan's largest sake-producing area.

full.name: Himeji
full.blurb: Japan's most magnificent original castle, a UNESCO 'White Heron' fortress, about 40 minutes west by Shinkansen.

full.name: Kyoto
full.blurb: The old imperial capital of temples, shrines, and geisha lanes, about an hour away by JR Special Rapid.

full.name: Osaka
full.blurb: Japan's brash 'kitchen', a 20-30 minute train ride away, for Dōtonbori, the castle, and street food.

full.name: Awaji Island
full.blurb: Reached across the world's longest suspension bridge, an island of beaches, flower parks, and the Naruto whirlpools.
